verdicts.reason: X measures the writer's own prior contact history with the agency while Y measures awareness of and joint action with other commenters, so a first-time joint filing scores high on Y and zero on X.
Both score evidence of a prior and ongoing relationship with the agency (earlier submissions, meetings, direct exchanges), differing only in how much citation detail the top anchor demands.
Both count the same costly document-production artifacts (exhibits, indexes, slide decks, attachment inventories) versus plain prose.

X credits any docket-lifecycle marker including extensions, supplemental filings, delayed transmission, and replies to other commenters, none of which imply the agency-personnel relationship Y requires.
Citing CFR parts and sections is a referencing practice, while arguing the rule exceeds statutory authority is a substantive legal claim; either can appear without the other.
Both ask whether the comment offers a concrete alternative regulatory design specific enough for the agency to implement.
Y rewards any organizational-size figures including revenue, staffing, and facilities, so a single large firm scores high on Y while X requires constituency or signatory breadth.

X keys on joint or coalition structure (named coalition, joint campaign, many signatories) whereas Y keys on sheer represented magnitude, so a single association touting millions of members scores high on Y and low on X.
The two rubrics list nearly identical cues (prior meetings, collaboration, earlier submissions, direct agency contacts) against an identical one-off-submission floor.
Emotional intensity and first-hand operational experience are independent: a practitioner can describe practice in flat register, and an outsider can be vehement without any experience.
Both count the same display of stacked degrees, certifications, fellowships, offices, and titles by the author or signatories.
Both require self-derived numeric compliance-cost figures with the basis or source stated, and both floor at no figures.
Both score whether the comment presents itself as a continuing exchange with the agency (prior filings, meetings, pending petitions, responses to agency questions) rather than a one-off contact.
